chapter_theme: The mullai decade of the Thinaimozhi Aimpathu (21-30, Kannan Chenthanar): in the rainy season the friend points the waiting heroine to the season's signs (the kaayaa, kodal and mullai in bloom, the thunder like kings' drums, the cloud drinking the sea, the deer with his doe, the herds dripping milk) as the token the absent man set for his return, and promises that her pallor will go; in 21 he has already come.

21.reading: The friend tells the heroine that her lover has come and her shoulders shine: the collyrium-dark kaayaa has bloomed, the kurukilai buds have taken the beauty of the smile of women with bright bangles, and the cool kodal has put out its ladle-shaped spathes.
21.nuance: Unlike the verses around it, this one reports the arrival as done (வந்தார், past), so the season's flowers are no longer a promise but the frame of the return; her shining shoulders are the pallor's undoing, said without naming the pallor. The women's smile is set inside the flower, so the woodland already smiles the smile the heroine will now smile.

thinai_evidence.note: the kaayaa and kodal in flower are the rain-season blossoms of the woodland

comparisons.tenor: the kaayaa blossom, dark as collyrium
the white kurukilai buds, given the beauty of women's smiles
the kodal spathe, shaped like a ladle

22.reading: The friend asks the heroine of the fine brow what will become now of the pallor that crept over her soft breasts, for here, she says, our man will come: this rain-cloud has made the season, with mullai of many colours in bud, and taken on its sweet colour.
22.nuance: The pallor is spoken of as a creeping thing (ஊர்ந்த) whose fate is now in question, so the friend's 'what will become of it' is a playful threat against the pallor rather than a question to the girl. The cloud is said to 'make' the season (பருவஞ்செய்து), as if keeping the man's appointment for him.

thinai_evidence.note: mullai in bud and the rain-cloud making the season

comparisons.tenor: the pallor as a thing that crawls over her breasts

23.reading: The friend tells the heroine of close-set bangles that he who went will come: here is the rain, thundering and roaring like the drums of fiercely angry kings, having drunk the flood of the cool sea and come to its height, and tomorrow it will be greater than today.
23.nuance: 'Tomorrow more than today' turns the friend's proof into a rising scale: each day's heavier rain is a nearer return. The kings' drum keeps the reason for his absence, the king's war or work, inside the sound that promises his coming.

thinai_evidence.note: the thundering rain-cloud that has drunk the sea

comparisons.tenor: the cloud as a drinker of the sea

24.reading: The friend tells the heroine, whose soft breasts bear red beauty spots, to let the pallor that has settled on her go: here is the woodland where the rain-sky, swelling with fierce anger, thundering and roaring, has poured its cool rain as the sign of the return of him who swore his oath and held to his resolve.
24.nuance: Two kinds of சினம் face each other: his வஞ்சினம், the sworn vow he made when he left, and the sky's வெஞ்சினம், fierce anger, so the storm reads as the vow made audible. The sign (குறி) is his, not the sky's: the rain is the token he named.

thinai_evidence.note: the rain-sky pouring on the woodland

comparisons.tenor: the rain-sky, swelling with anger as it thunders

25.reading: As the massed dark rain-clouds, mingling with the wind, rise up, and the tender young buck leaps with his doe, the friend tells the heroine of lovely breasts that our lover will come right now, at the time he resolved on.
25.nuance: Strike line 2 and the friend's word stands: the rains have come and he will come now, at the time he set. The buck with his doe is the one thing in the verse that acts as a lover should, which is why it can comfort.

thinai_evidence.note: the rain-clouds and the deer at play with his doe in the woodland

iraicchi.act: the young buck leaps and plays together with his doe in the first rains
iraicchi.sense: the creatures keep their mates beside them in this season, so the man who fixed this time will be beside her now

26.reading: The friend says this is the time he told us of, fittingly, when he made the sign of his return: the beautiful cloud that drank the dark sea has thundered so that the curling mullai creeper grows lovely, and the great rain hangs low.
26.nuance: பொருந்த, 'fittingly', says the season and his word now match: the friend's proof is the agreement of the two, not the rain alone. The poem names the moment of his speaking (நமக்குரைத்த போழ்து), so the friend counts herself among those he promised.

thinai_evidence.note: mullai made lovely by the thundering cloud and the heavy rain

comparisons.tenor: the cloud as a drinker of the sea

27.reading: The friend points to the bewildering evening, when the herdsmen move their herds home, the cloud, having scooped water from the deep sea, thunders to spread far, and the vast dark world fills with darkness, as the sign that he who went on his work set for his return.
27.nuance: The mullai evening, which elsewhere torments the waiting woman, is here turned by the friend into his appointed token. The verse gives no vocative, so who speaks is inferred from the run of the decade.

thinai_evidence.note: herdsmen driving the herds home in the rainy evening

comparisons.tenor: the cloud scooping water from the sea like a vessel

28.reading: The friend says that, as the cloud with its thunder of shaking voice drinks the wave-tossed sea and roars so that the serpent with its ripe gem cowers, and in the evening that hides the sun the heavy rain hangs low, the beauty spots will spread over her breasts.
28.nuance: The spots (சுணங்கு) on a woman's breasts are a sign of happiness and union, the opposite of the pallor of the other verses; the friend predicts the body's change from waiting to joy. The gem-bearing serpent that shrinks at thunder is a stock belief of the rains.

thinai_evidence.note: the thunder and heavy rain of the evening

comparisons.tenor: the cloud as a drinker of the sea

29.reading: The friend calls the heroine of fine jewels to come out and see the woodland with her: the rain has made the whole forest its own, the sharp buds of the lovely kodal look like snakes ready to strike, the mullai has put out buds, and fine sand flows down every stream.
29.nuance: The proof is no longer reported but shared: 'come, let us see' (போதராய் காண்பாம்) invites the heroine out of the house into the season itself. The same words could be the returned man's to his wife; the run of the decade favours the friend.

thinai_evidence.note: the forest taken over by the rains and the mullai in bud

comparisons.tenor: the sharp kodal buds, like snakes raising their hoods to strike

30.reading: The friend tells the heroine of the striped-bangled arm that this rain has bloomed in full, the cloud thundering in grace, the kurukilai flowering and the chosen herds of cows oozing sweet milk; will our man not come?
30.nuance: 'Will our man come?' (வருவார் நமர்கொல்) is a question whose answer the whole season has given; the cows streaming milk for their calves are the plainest picture of a return home, though the verse draws no match, so they stay scene.

thinai_evidence.note: cows dripping milk and the woodland in flower in the rains

comparisons.tenor: the rain-season spoken of as a flower in full bloom

links.note: Kar Narpathu 8: the woodland where the kaayaa opens buds as if dipped in the collyrium of an eye announces the return of the man who went for fame. Thinaimozhi Aimpathu 21: with the collyrium-dark kaayaa in bloom, the lover has come.
links.teaches: The same collyrium-blue kaayaa that in the Kar Narpathu is still only a herald of the man becomes, in the Thinaimozhi verse, the flower already open when he arrives, so the mullai venbas use one stock blossom to mark both the promise and its keeping.

links.note: Thinaimozhi Aimpathu 22: the friend asks what will become of the pallor now that the rain says he will come. Kural 1265: the woman says the pallor of her shoulders will leave only after she has seen her husband with full eyes; on a plain reading they disagree on whether news of his return can touch the pallor.
links.teaches: The friend treats the pallor as already beaten by the season's promise, while the couplet's woman refuses any cure short of seeing him, so the couplet sounds like the heroine's unspoken reply to the friend's teasing question.

links.note: Both liken the thundering rain to the drums of kings (வேந்தர் ... முரசின்). Kuruntokai 380: the friend says their lover is in a far country, not before them; how shall they bear it? Thinaimozhi Aimpathu 23: the friend says he who went will come, and the rain will be greater tomorrow.
links.teaches: One image, the sky beating like a king's drum, serves the friend once as proof that he is coming and once as a measure of how far away he still is, which shows that in the rains the friend's comfort is a choice of reading, not a fact the season settles.

links.note: Thinaimozhi Aimpathu 24: the friend rests her comfort on the man who swore an oath (வஞ்சினம்) and held to it, with the rain as his token. Kural 1154: if he who said 'fear not' leaves, is there any fault in those who trusted his assuring word?
links.teaches: The friend builds her comfort on his oath, while the couplet asks who is to blame if such an oath fails, so together they show that the whole mullai argument of waiting rests on trusting a man's word, and the Kural names the risk the friend leaves unsaid.

links.note: Akananuru 74: the heroine says she could hold firm on the friend's repeated comfort (he will see the doe with the stag in the rain-fresh scrub, think of you and come today, இன்றே வருவர்) if only the herdsmen's harsh little flute did not torment her at evening. Thinaimozhi Aimpathu 25: the friend points to the buck leaping with his doe and says he will come right now (இன்னே வருவர்).
links.teaches: The Thinaimozhi verse gives the friend's argument by itself, and the Akananuru heroine quotes that same argument and tells us where it breaks, at evening with the flute, so the four-line comfort is shown as one turn of a longer exchange in which it does not fully hold.

links.note: Kuruntokai 21: though the forest's konrai says it is the rainy season, the heroine will not believe it, for he does not lie. Thinaimozhi Aimpathu 26: the friend says the thundering rain is the time he named, fitting his word.
links.teaches: Both trust the man's word, but they draw opposite conclusions from it: the friend reads the rain as his promise kept, the Kuruntokai woman reads his absence as proof the rain is not yet the true season, so the same faith can either confirm the season or deny it.

links.note: Both name the bewildering evening (மருண்மாலை, மருள்மாலை). Kural 1222: the woman asks the sad-eyed evening whether its partner is as hard-hearted as hers. Thinaimozhi Aimpathu 27: the friend calls the darkening rainy evening the sign the man set for his return.
links.teaches: The same evening the Kural's woman mourns as a fellow sufferer abandoned like herself is presented by the friend as the very token of his return, which shows that the evening's meaning in love poetry depends on who is speaking and whether she still trusts him.

links.note: Both have the thunder (ஏறு) make the gem-bearing serpent cower (மணி நாகம் அனுங்க) as the rain-cloud goes. Kar Narpathu 20: the returning man tells his charioteer the king's work is done. Thinaimozhi Aimpathu 28: the friend tells the heroine the beauty spots will spread on her breasts.
links.teaches: A near-identical half-line serves at both ends of the journey, in the returning man's mouth and in the waiting woman's friend's, which shows the serpent cowering at the thunder as a shared formula of the mullai rains rather than one poet's image.

links.note: Akananuru 14: in the evening when good cows with swollen udders ooze sweet milk (தீம்பால் பிலிற்ற) and call to their calves, the wife asks the bard how she will be at dawn if he does not remember them; the bard then sees the chariot coming. Thinaimozhi Aimpathu 30: with the herds oozing sweet milk (தீம்பால் பிலிற்ற), the friend asks 'will our man come?'
links.teaches: The same phrase of cows streaming milk carries the question of his return in both poems, and the long Akananuru supplies the answer the venba leaves open, the chariot on the road, so the milk-heavy herd going home is a fixed cue that the man too must be on his way.

source_issues: 21-30: the colophon gives the thinai (முல்லை) but no thurai; the speaker (thozhi) and addressee (thalaivi) are inferred from the verses' vocatives, so occasion words are null.
27 line 1: ஆம்பல் அடைதாய் is hard to construe (the ambal flute tune of the herdsmen, or the water-lily leaf?); line 4 செயவர் is probably சேயவர், the one far away. The verse is marked uncertain.
28 line 4: கணங்கு reads as a misprint for சுணங்கு, the beauty spots (compare 24 line 1, செஞ்சுணங்கின்). The verse is marked uncertain.
30 line 3: வரிவனைத் is a misprint for வரிவளைத், striped bangles; line 1 அருளி and line 2 தெரிஆ are unclear, and the verse is marked uncertain.
26 line 2: சுருங்கொடி may be சுரும்கொடி or a curling creeper; taken as the mullai creeper.
